body.text: The academic and author Edward Glaeser, who is the Fred and Eleanor Glimp Professor of Economics in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences at Harvard University, has consistently argued that cities become prosperous not because of grand physical infrastructure alone but because they enable the exchange of ideas, talent, and entrepreneurship. In this email interview with Frontline, Prof. Glaeser, who is the author of Triumph of the City (2011) and the co-author of Survival of the City (2022), shares his views on varied topics, including agglomeration economics, housing regulation, land-use policy, and urban governance. Edited excerpts:

India has made infrastructure the centrepiece of its economic strategy, investing heavily in highways, airports, freight corridors, and urban transport. From the perspective of urban economics, are these the investments that generate the greatest long-term returns, or should India be prioritising different kinds of infrastructure?

These can be high-return investments, but they can also be wasteful white elephants. Two hundred and fifty years ago, Adam Smith, the father of economics, extolled the virtues of financing infrastructure with user fees. He made the point—and it is still true today—that building infrastructure only when users can be expected to cover its costs is a great way to ensure that we build sensibly. While I accept that this ideal may be impossible in many contexts, both because of the difficulties of charging users and because equity considerations preclude imposing such charges on the poor, I remain convinced that we should strive to rely on user-fee financing as often as possible. This is particularly true for infrastructure used by businesses, like freight corridors, and infrastructure used predominantly by richer people, like airports.

Without user-fee financing, it is still possible to use cost-benefit analysis to guide us towards high return investment. Costs should include both financial costs and any damage to the environment. Benefits would include direct benefits to transportation users and possibly benefits to other entities, such as employers. Naturally, this analysis can be altered so that benefits for the poor are weighted more highly than benefits for the rich. Without a serious set of such analyses, it is impossible to make any general statements about these investments in physical infrastructure. Certainly, in the US context, we believe that much of the early highway investments were high return and many of the more recent investments were not. I should emphasise that I also believe that the returns to human capital are higher than the returns to investment in physical capital and this is particularly true in India. Schools, especially for the youngest Indians, generate huge returns, and these should certainly be prioritised. Human capital is the bedrock on which sits the success of cities, people, and nations.

India is expected to add hundreds of millions of people to its urban population over the coming decades. Is this demographic shift an economic opportunity or a governance challenge, and what will determine which way it goes?

The growth of India’s cities is both an economic opportunity and a governance challenge. Wages (and self-reported happiness) are both much higher in India’s cities than in rural areas. Cities provide pathways out of poverty into prosperity that are transforming the world. India should embrace its urbanisation and accept that the growth of cities will enable its economy to grow and provide opportunity for millions of new workers.

That being said, there are also demons that come with density. Traffic congestion, contagious disease, high housing prices, and crime are all occasional companions of urban growth. These problems can be handled with sensible public policies. Sewers and vaccination work against disease. Congestion pricing and good road paving increase road speeds. But these policies require strong governments. Singapore, for example, is particularly effective at dealing with the densities of big city life. Traditionally, Indian cities have been hampered in their ability to deal with these challenges by a lack of local control. Often State governments, which can be dominated by rural legislators, have controlled the tools needed to improve quality of life in urban areas. Strong and accountable local governments can help ensure that city growth improves both incomes and quality of life.

One of your central arguments is that housing shortages are often policy failures rather than market failures. Indian cities face soaring land prices alongside widespread informal settlements. What are the biggest policy distortions you see?

I have long been a critic of floor-area requirements that limit the growth of Indian buildings and that ensure that there is too much space between the towers that do appear. One story that is often told is that planners in the 1960s wanted to use land-use regulations to limit the growth of cities. Their efforts failed and only ensured that growth would occur in informal settlements rather than formal high-rise buildings. I would like it to be easy to build in India and for regulations to be limited to health and safety. I would also like to see a pedestrian agenda that prioritises foot travel. I see this as involving both less regulation of the private sector and a robust public sector focus on making mobility easier.

I don’t want to prioritise one regulation versus another. There are an enormous number of ways to say no to a building project. The key is to have an empowered local leader who has the ability to enable growth and the incentives to make that happen.

As climate risks intensify, Indian cities are facing floods, heatwaves, and water stress with increasing frequency. How should urban infrastructure planning incorporate climate resilience without slowing economic growth?

While I am incredibly confident in my recommendation to make Indian building regulations more permissive, I am quite reticent about making strong advice related to climate change adaptation. I believe that this is incredibly important and incredibly hard. Limits on state capacity can also make things particularly change. For example, if a city can’t stop people from moving into a floodplain, then it is far more likely that the city is going to experience water-related deaths.

I am sure that Indian cities will continue to be on the front line of the battle to save their citizens from the ravages of water and heat that come with climate change. Drainage is important and so is access to air-conditioned facilities for vulnerable populations. I have been part of a learning group that is trying to understand these challenges better, and I hope that in a year or two, I will have more to share.
Indian cities have invested heavily in metro rail systems. Yet congestion remains severe. Are cities paying too much attention to mobility infrastructure and too little to land-use planning?

There is an old joke that 40 years of transportation economics at Harvard can be boiled down to four words: “bus good, train bad.” This advice reflected both the extremely high costs of metro systems and the much greater flexibility of bus systems. Bus rapid transit systems provide a less expensive alternative to trains that works well in cities like Curitiba and Bogota. That being said, India’s cities are extremely dense, and it is quite possible that the metro systems do satisfy cost-benefit analysis.

But I also believe that India is not doing enough to push buildings together and allow high densities along walking corridors. Manhattan is a great model, and so is London. Singapore and Shanghai also work well. Tall buildings that are close together provide a much better mobility model than sprawl connected by trains. Moreover, India is also not doing enough to limit traffic within the existing grid. Congestion pricing provides a great way to reduce congestions. It was pioneered by Singapore in 1975, when Singapore was still a poor place. New York, London, and Stockholm all have congestion charges, and it is helpful everywhere. My colleague Gabriel Kreindler also finds that road roughness has a major impact on reducing traffic speeds in India, which suggests that better repaving practices can also speed the flow of traffic.

India’s cities contribute a disproportionately large share of GDP, yet urban local bodies remain financially and administratively weak. How much does governance matter compared with physical infrastructure?

Strong governance is a complement to physical infrastructure. We only get good infrastructure when the government is effective. We only get good infrastructure maintenance and management when it is managed by an effective entity. Getting stronger institutions in Indian cities seems like a particularly important objective to me.

Countries such as China, South Korea, and Vietnam urbanised rapidly while simultaneously building globally competitive manufacturing sectors. Why has India’s urbanisation followed a different trajectory?

India is hardly unique. Latin America and now Africa are also experiencing urbanisation without globally competitive manufacturing. One challenge is that the East Asians are just incredibly good at producing tradeable goods. Their wages may now be higher, but their productive capital makes it hard to compete with them. The US is in the same boat. The amazing thing, which India is proving, is that urbanisation and economic growth can still occur without globally competitive manufacturing. I think India should embrace that path that it is on, and try to make sure that its governments do all they can to create a strong business environment and a high quality of life in the country’s urban areas.

India has invested significantly in digital public infrastructure. Can digital infrastructure compensate for deficiencies in physical urban infrastructure, or are they complements rather than substitutes?

I tend to think that they are complements rather than substitutes. Digital infrastructure enables you to order something online, but you still need that thing to be delivered live. There are settings where the ability to telecommute can substitute for using the roads, but I think that these are relatively rare. The more important effect is that a more digitally sophisticated world will also be a more interactive world, and some of those interactions will happen live and need physical infrastructure.
If you were writing a sequel to Triumph of the City focussed on India, what would its central argument be?

I would put more emphasis on the battle to curb the downsides of density. There would be a whole chapter on water and sanitary infrastructure. I might also have a chapter of entrepreneurship, with a special focus on female entrepreneurship. There is a whole research agenda about gender and the city that I am very excited about.
